sections.title: Keys: Lesson 13, Foundation models and representations

keyTerms.definition: Models pretrained on broad data and then adapted to downstream tasks.
Feature maps learned by pretraining and reused across tasks.

recall.question: Which two topics do the Lesson 13 keys cover?

keyTerms.definition: Average loss over broad, usually unlabeled data, in the first of two phases.
A linear classifier trained on frozen pretrained features.
A low-rank weight update Delta W equals BA with trainable count r(d_out plus d_in).
A positive pair is two augmentations of the same image; a negative pair uses a different image.
A loss that pulls positive pairs together and pushes negative pairs apart.
Recall at k and NDCG at k, which measure ranked retrieval quality.

recall.question: What are the two phases of foundation-model training?
recall.answer: Pretraining on broad, usually unlabeled data, then adaptation to downstream tasks.

recall.question: How many trainable parameters does a LoRA update have?
recall.answer: r(d_out plus d_in), for Delta W equals BA with rank r.

recall.question: What makes a contrastive loss decrease?
recall.answer: It decreases when a positive inner product grows and increases when a negative inner product grows.

keyTerms.definition: With 200 examples a probe is safe and convex; finetuning can win but risks distortion; LP-FT is the hedge.
Damage from too large a learning rate on too few examples.
The numeric check that loss falls from 3.4603 to 3.3709 when positives move closer.
Collapse when there is no negative pressure or no stop-gradient in a symmetric architecture.

recall.question: What is the hedge between probing and finetuning?
recall.answer: LP-FT: start with a linear probe, then finetune, so distortion risk is limited while gains are kept.

recall.question: When do random pairs hurt contrastive learning?
recall.answer: Random pairs can be false negatives, so the loss pushes apart same-class items.

keyTerms.definition: The derivative in p is negative and in q is positive, so positives attract and negatives repel.
NDCG at 4 is 0.9305 from DCG at 4 of 4.4307 over IDCG at 4 of 4.7619.

recall.question: What is NDCG at 4 in the worked example?
recall.answer: DCG at 4 is 4.4307, IDCG at 4 is 4.7619, so NDCG at 4 is 0.9305.

keyTerms.definition: The retriever misses but the generator answers anyway.
Requiring the generator to say the answer is not in the passages instead of hallucinating.

recall.question: How do you fix a generator that answers from bad retrieval?
recall.answer: Add a retrieval eval with Recall at k, surface scores, and require abstention or citation grounding.

keyTerms.definition: 40 full weight copies with 40x serving memory and no sharing.
One base plus 40 small adapters with fast swapping and near-simultaneous serving.

recall.question: When does full finetuning beat adapters?
recall.answer: When tasks are far from pretraining so large shifts need full-rank updates, or when latency forbids even adapter swapping.

keyTerms.definition: As distribution shift grows, the OOD gap between LP-FT and plain finetuning shrinks and vanishes past a stated shift level.
The out-of-distribution difference between LP-FT and plain finetuning.

recall.question: Why would the LP-FT gap vanish under large shift?
recall.answer: Because the probe initialization no longer constrains the needed feature change.

keyTerms.definition: SIMCLR loss 3.4603 to 3.3709, LoRA counts match the rank table, Recall at k and NDCG at k match hand computation.
The trainable count matches r(d_out plus d_in) for the rank table.

recall.question: What verifies the lab-07 implementation?
recall.answer: The SIMCLR loss moves 3.4603 to 3.3709 when positives move closer, LoRA counts match the rank table, and Recall at k and NDCG at k match hand computation.
